“The Sirens: it seems they did indeed sing, but in an unfulfilling way, one that only gave a sign of where the real sources and real happiness of song opened.” (p. 3)
“it was also a means of navigation” (p. 4)
“His is a fortunate and secure cowardliness, based on privilege, which places him outside of the common condition” (p. 4)
“After the Sirens had been conquered by the power of the technique that always tries to play safely with unreal (inspired) powers” (p. 5)
“We cannot deny that Ulysses heard a little of what Ahab saw, but he held firm in the midst of hearing” (p. 8)
“The presence of a song only still to come.” (p. 9)
“Mallarmé calls the reader ‘the operator.’” (p. 242)
fields.Themes: Sirens, Ulysses, Homer, Ahab, narrative, imaginary, song to come, technique, privilege, oarsmen, Mallarmé, Livre, operator

fields.Title: The Architecture of Madness: Insane Asylums in the United States
fields.Author: Carla Yanni
fields.Role_in_Set: Anchor — the plan
fields.Selection_Logic: Architectural history outside recent literary-theory sets; supplies the Kirkbride plan the other two distort and names the mechanism (ward as reward/punishment) that makes the triad cohere.
fields.Quotes: "For most of the nineteenth century, doctors believed that between 70 and 90 percent of insanity cases were curable, but only if patients were treated in specially designed buildings." (Intro, p. 1) | "(A patient did not need the asylum to be a lunatic, but a doctor needed the asylum to be a psychiatrist.)" (Intro, p. 7) | "The Kirkbride plan, also known as the linear plan, was a type of congregate plan, made up of short but connected pavilions, arrayed in a shallow V." (p. 51) | "These wards would be used to categorize patients by severity of disease, with the noisiest patients farthest away from the center." (p. 60) | "But the classification system was also a management device—a transfer to a nicer ward was a reward for a well-behaved patient. Relocation to a lower ward was a punishment." (p. 64) | "The interior space of the asylum was strictly hierarchical, and patients were constantly aware of their place within the numerical wards." (p. 65)
fields.Themes: Kirkbride plan, moral treatment, classification, ward hierarchy, AMSAII, asylum size, patient accounts

fields.Title: The Alienist
fields.Author: Joaquim Maria Machado de Assis (trans. William L. Grossman per publisher)
fields.Role_in_Set: The theory — the classifier who ends inside
fields.Selection_Logic: Satire of the same machine from the doctor's side: the Green House's boundary redrawn until the town, then the balanced (sorted into galleries by virtue), then the doctor are inside; written in the decades Yanni covers.
fields.Quotes: "“Science,” he told His Majesty, “is my only office; Itaguai, my universe.”" (ch. I) | "The building had a courtyard in the center and two hundred cubicles, each with one window." (ch. I) | "At the end of four months the Green House was a little community in itself. A gallery with thirty-seven more cubicles had to be added." (ch. II) | "Till now, madness has been thought a small island in an ocean of sanity. I am beginning to suspect that it is not an island at all but a continent." (ch. IV) | "In one gallery lived only those whose outstanding moral quality was modesty." (ch. XII) | "He entered the Green House, shut the door behind him, and set about the business of curing himself." (ch. XIII)
fields.Themes: Green House, Bacamarte, Itaguai, equilibrium, classification, galleries of virtue, inversion of doctrine, self-commitment

fields.Title: Down Below
fields.Author: Leonora Carrington (intro. Marina Warner)
fields.Role_in_Set: The inmate — the plan read as cosmology
fields.Selection_Logic: The patient's view Yanni says is scarce; Carrington maps Dr. Morales's pavilions onto Egypt/China/Jerusalem, getting the ward-as-reward ladder right in the wrong vocabulary.
fields.Quotes: "Exactly three years ago, I was interned in Dr. Morales’s sanatorium in Santander, Spain, Dr. Pardo, of Madrid, and the British Consul having pronounced me incurably insane." (23 Aug 1943) | "(By looking at the map, you will see the respective positions of Villa Pilar, Radiografia, Covadonga, Amachu, and Abajo (Down Below); that will enable you to get your bearings.)" (24 Aug 1943) | "The pavilion with this name was for me the Earth, the Real World, Paradise, Eden, Jerusalem." (26 Aug 1943) | "I realized that I had to find my place in the circle, and sat at 45 degrees to the left of the door" (27 Aug 1943) | "that Covadonga and Amachu and Down Below were not Egypt, China, and Jerusalem, but pavilions for the insane and that I should get out as quickly as possible." (27 Aug 1943) | Excerpt: “Is Down Below nice?” “Delightful. Everyone is happy there.” “Take me with you.” “I can’t.” “Why not?” “Because you’re not well enough to go there.” (25 Aug 1943)
fields.Themes: Santander, Dr. Morales, Cardiazol, Down Below/Abajo, Covadonga, Amachu, Sun Room, pavilions as cosmology, demystification, surrealism

fields.Title: The Ignorant Schoolmaster: Five Lessons in Intellectual Emancipation
fields.Author: Jacques Rancière (trans. Kristin Ross)
fields.Role_in_Set: Anchor: the case for the ignorant master and the equality of intelligences.
fields.Selection_Logic: Strongest modern argument that one can teach what one does not know; its target, the explicator, is Steiner's Master; its examples (illiterate father, Lord's Prayer, pupil teaching teacher) are what Williams documents, criminalized, in the same decades.
fields.Quotes: "There is stultification whenever one intelligence is subordinated to another." (p. 13) | "There is no one on earth who hasn't learned something by himself and without a master explicator." (p. 16) | "Whoever teaches without emancipating stultifies." (p. 18) | "To teach what one doesn't know is simply to ask questions about what one doesn't know." (p. 30) | "Universal teaching is the poor's method. But it isn't a method of the poor." (p. 106) | "It's the disciple that makes the master." (p. 19) | Excerpt pp. 29–30 (Meno's slave)
fields.Themes: Jacotot, universal teaching, explication, stultification, equality of intelligence, Télémaque, Meno, ignorant master

fields.Title: Lessons of the Masters
fields.Author: George Steiner
fields.Role_in_Set: Opponent: the eloquent defense of mastery and discipleship.
fields.Selection_Logic: Reads the Meno against Rancière (Socrates makes autodidacts; the slave boy's proof is unsound); names in one sentence that 'Master' carries the stain of slavery and sets American self-made talent against the magisterium.
fields.Quotes: "Masters have destroyed their disciples both psychologically and, in rarer cases, physically." (Intro) | "The Master learns from the disciple and is modified by this interrelation in what becomes, ideally, a process of exchange." (Intro) | "Exemplary teaching is enactment and can be mute. Perhaps it ought to be." (Intro) | "One might say that whoever grasps Socrates's intention is made an autodidact, especially in ethics." (ch. 1) | "And it has been shown that the geometrical proof that Socrates elicits by his midwifery from the slave boy in Meno is unsound." (ch. 1) | "The very word 'Master' carries the stain of slavery." (ch. 5)
fields.Themes: mastery, discipleship, eros of teaching, betrayal, refusal to teach, Socrates, Meno, Norton Lectures, America

fields.Title: Self-Taught: African American Education in Slavery and Freedom
fields.Author: Heather Andrea Williams
fields.Role_in_Set: Ground: learning and teaching without masters, under law that forbade both.
fields.Selection_Logic: Jacotot's ignorant masters in fact (native schools taught by people who had only just learned to read); the antiliteracy statutes (1819–1834 cluster) fall inside Jacotot's career; the 'self-made' that Steiner names, at its real cost.
fields.Quotes: "What learning dey would get in dem days, dey been get it at night. Taught demselves." (Louisa Gause, ch. 1 epigraph) | "Some slaves copied letters and words whose meanings they could not yet decipher onto fences and in the dirt." (ch. 1) | "Some young man, some woman, or old preacher, in cellar, or shed, or corner of a Negro meeting-house, with the alphabet in hand, or a torn spelling-book, is their teacher." (Alvord, ch. 6) | "Teaching amounted to a political act for African Americans in the emancipation period. And it was an act of courage." (ch. 6) | "But why have a Freedman's Primer any more than a Dutchman's Primer or an Irishman's Primer?" (ch. 7 epigraph) | Excerpt ch. 1 (pit schools) | Appendix: NC 1830–31 'the use of figures excepted'
fields.Themes: slave literacy, pit schools, native schools, antiliteracy statutes, freedpeople's schools, Black teachers, spelling books, Freedman's Primer

fields.Title: In Praise of Shadows
fields.Author: Jun'ichirō Tanizaki (trans. Gregory Starr)
fields.Role_in_Set: Anchor: makes the value of time's mark concrete, then undercuts it ('just dirt'); the only one of the three for whom the mark comes from use and touch.
fields.Selection_Logic: Concrete catalogue of things improved by tarnish and darkness; the scolded maid who polished the silver is the triad's emblem; 'Final grumblings' restates Kenkō's §22 knowingly; Gothic spire vs. eave answers Ruskin's architecture.
fields.Quotes:
"Every household has experienced a time when the master has had to scold a maid who unwittingly polished a silver bowl just as it finally gained an elegant patina." (p. 29)
"This “sheen of antiquity” that we hear so much about is, in reality, just dirt." (p. 32)
"the caress of a hand in the same place smooths the surface as the oil from the skin permeates the ceramics. It is this that creates the sheen—so in other words, yes, it’s just dirt." (p. 32)
"Indeed, to build a Japanese home, we first open an umbrella to create shade over the location, and in the dim light of that shadow we construct our house." (p. 43)
"The elders of the last century yearned for the era of two centuries ago; those of two centuries ago longed for that of three centuries ago—the conclusion being that those of any era will not be satisfied with the present." (p. 78)
"I would deepen the eaves of the temple of literature, darken its walls and push all things ostentatious into the darkness, stripping all unnecessary decorations from the interior." (p. 83)
fields.Themes: shadow, patina, tarnish, nare, lacquer, candlelight, electric light, eaves, zuihitsu, nostalgia

fields.Title: Essays in Idleness
fields.Author: Yoshida Kenkō (trans. G. B. Sansom)
fields.Role_in_Set: Ancestor and hinge: the native source of Tanizaki's taste for the worn and incomplete, and the Buddhist position from which Ruskin's anxious preservation looks like attachment.
fields.Selection_Logic: §81 'an air of age', §82 'It is incompleteness that is desirable' and the palace's unfinished place, §22 regret for the past, §13/§191 lamplight; the preface's 'without order or purpose' grounds the zuihitsu/architextuality link.
fields.Quotes:
"To while away the idle hours, seated the livelong day before the ink-slab, by jotting down without order or purpose whatever trifling thoughts pass through my mind, verily this is a queer and crazy thing to do!" (preface)
"Truly the beauty of life is its uncertainty." (§7)
"In all things one looks back with regret to the past. Modern fashions appear to be growing from bad to worse." (§22)
"What one wants are things with an air of age, not showy and expensive, but of good quality." (§81)
"To leave a thing unfinished gives interest, and makes for lengthened life. They say that even in building the palace an unfinished place is always left." (§82)
"Are we only to look at flowers in full bloom, at the moon when clear?" (§137)
fields.Themes: impermanence, incompleteness, air of age, lamplight, zuihitsu, regret for the past, Buddhist recluse

fields.Title: The Lamp of Memory
fields.Author: John Ruskin
fields.Role_in_Set: Western, moral counterpart: age as the glory of a building and the 'golden stain of time'; the sharpest opposite to Tanizaki's handled sheen, a prohibition on touching.
fields.Selection_Logic: 'Its glory is in its Age'; restoration 'a Lie from beginning to end'; 'They are not ours.' The Penguin Great Ideas text elides (with '…') the picturesque / 'Parasitical Sublimity' section, the part closest to Tanizaki.
fields.Quotes:
"For, indeed, the greatest glory of a building is not in its stones, nor in its gold. Its glory is in its Age" (¶11)
"it is in that golden stain of time, that we are to look for the real light, and colour, and preciousness of architecture" (¶11)
"Do not let us talk then of restoration. The thing is a Lie from beginning to end." (¶12)
"Watch an old building with an anxious care; guard it as best you may, and at any cost, from every influence of dilapidation." (¶12)
"They are not ours. They belong partly to those who built them, and partly to all the generations of mankind who are to follow us." (¶13)
"This closing paragraph of the sixth chapter is the best, I think, in the book, – and the vainest. [1880.]" (note)
fields.Themes: memory, age-value, golden stain, restoration, preservation, picturesque, railway, inheritance, the dead's rights

fields.Title: A Perfect Vacuum
fields.Author: Stanisław Lem (trans. Michael Kandel)
fields.Role_in_Set: Anchor: the impossible blank book, reviewed; the extreme position (nothing reached only by language's self-annihilation)
fields.Selection_Logic: The 'Rien du tout, ou la consequence' review is a pure thought experiment: a novel of total negation whose critic admits the reader supplies everything (railway station, erotic encounter). Supplies the review form and the claim that a decent literature must cease rather than end.
fields.Quotes:
"It was necessary, then—and herein is the consequence—to write nothing." (p. 71)
"Total freedom is total paralysis in literature." (p. 72)
"Instead of a print we obtain an exact negative, that is all. The nature of an innovation must be ontological, and not simply grammatical!" (p. 74)
"Nonbeing is already known to us in literature, but only as a certain Lack—of Something—for Someone." (p. 75)
"How can a thing be in bad taste which is not there at all?!" (p. 76)
"The novel does not end: it ceases." (p. 79)
"a critique of a book that not only does not exist but also cannot." (p. 4)
fields.Themes: imaginary books, pseudo-review, negation, antinovel, nouveau roman, Solange Marriot, reader's responsibility, erotics of the blank, Borges's Pierre Menard, Barthes degree zero, ontological vs grammatical nothing

fields.Title: No Medium
fields.Author: Craig Dworkin
fields.Role_in_Set: Empirical counterweight: real blank works read closely; denies any true blank
fields.Selection_Logic: Where Lem invents his blank book, Dworkin catalogues real ones (Nudisme, Saroyan, Rauschenberg, Friedman's erased centerfold, silent records). His 'Further Listening' reviews empty records in a consumer-guide voice, Lem's form inverted. Thesis: 'there are no real absences, only replacements'; media are social acts of reading.
fields.Quotes:
"the difference between the sophistication of getting the joke and the greater sophistication of refusing to get the joke depends on how closely one reads a work that seems to ask only that it not be read." (ch. 1)
"Media—if there are such things—are only recognizable as collectives." (ch. 1)
"to resist falling back on the sensational metaphysics of either a reified nothingness or the poststructural apotheosis of absence and lack" (ch. 1)
"there are no real absences, only replacements" (ch. 2, Cenography)
"Those blank pages linked with the cosmos: space before creation." (Little Review reader, quoted ch. 1)
"The other five tracks are inconsequential, and the title track performance of 4'33" reveals the conductor doesn't take the tempi as marked; it clocks in a full 18 seconds too slow" (ch. 8, Further Listening)
fields.Themes: blank page, substrate, medium, Nudisme, Cocteau, Orphée, erasure, Rauschenberg, White Paintings, Cage, 4'33", silent records, discography, Saroyan, Tom Friedman, Little Review, Sterne's blank page

fields.Title: Some Ways of Making Nothing: Apophatic Apparatuses in Contemporary Art
fields.Author: Curt Cloninger
fields.Role_in_Set: Theory: a taxonomy of nothings and an ethics of making them; argues with both Lem (no permanent nothing) and Dworkin (nothing can be made, as braking)
fields.Selection_Logic: Supplies the theory the other two dispute: making nothing as purposeful braking of becoming, distinct from abstaining. Taxonomy (transcendent, bereft, fecund, deferred) lets Rien du tout and Dworkin's blanks be sorted. Brings negative theology and quantum apparatus (Barad, delayed-choice eraser) into the set.
fields.Quotes:
"There is, however, an important difference between abstaining from making something and purposefully making nothing." (p. 130)
"You cannot approach nothing; for there is nothing to approach." (Whitehead, quoted p. 130)
"A successful apophatic art apparatus is a work of art that resists (however fleetingly) the inevitable move toward becoming." (p. 143)
"Neither kataphasis nor apophasis ever get the last word." (p. 143)
"To equate blackness with nothing is to suffer from oculo-centrism" (p. 225)
"Some nothings leave you pointing west, some leave you pointing east, and some leave you spinning your wheels in a ditch." (p. 421)
fields.Themes: apophasis, kataphasis, Pseudo-Dionysius, Marion, Whitehead, Barad, apparatus, quantum eraser, Fludd hyle diagram, black square, Arakawa and Gins, bereft nothing, fecund nothing, perpetual deferment, ethics of nothing, braking becoming

fields.Title: Translations
fields.Author: Brian Friel
fields.Role_in_Set: Anchor: the scene the other two books theorize (1833 Name-Book; a closed speech-community opened by translation)
fields.Selection_Logic: A play about translation written entirely in English; dramatizes the Ordnance Survey's Anglicising of Irish place names and voices Steiner's theory of the private core through Hugh and Yolland.
fields.Quotes:
"Owen – Roland – what the hell. It’s only a name. It’s the same me, isn’t it? Well, isn’t it?" (Act One)
"I may learn the password but the language of the tribe will always elude me, won’t it? The private core will always be … hermetic, won’t it?" (Yolland, Act Two, Scene One)
"But remember that words are signals, counters. They are not immortal. And it can happen – to use an image you’ll understand – it can happen that a civilisation can be imprisoned in a linguistic contour which no longer matches the landscape of … fact." (Hugh, Act Two, Scene One)
"it is not the literal past, the ‘facts’ of history, that shape us, but images of the past embodied in language." (Hugh, Act Three)
"I will provide you with the available words and the available grammar. But will that help you to interpret between privacies?" (Hugh, Act Three)
fields.Themes: Name-Book, Ordnance Survey, Anglicisation, interpreter as censor, Tobair Vree, password, private core, Aeneid

fields.Title: After Babel: Aspects of Language and Translation
fields.Author: George Steiner
fields.Role_in_Set: Source: the theory Friel borrowed close to verbatim (genealogy edge)
fields.Selection_Logic: Friel drew on it while writing Translations; its thesis that speech matured through concealment ('All developed language has a private core'; the word as 'pass-word') frames Shelta as well. Second edition with 1992 preface.
fields.Quotes:
"A civilization is imprisoned in a linguistic contour which no longer matches, or matches only at certain ritual, arbitrary points, the changing landscape of fact." (Ch. 1)
"Languages are wholly arbitrary sets of signals and conventionalized counters." (Ch. 1)
"Often, cultures seem to expend on their vocabulary and syntax acquisitive energies and ostentations entirely lacking in their material lives." (Ch. 2)
"Obviously, we speak to communicate. But also to conceal, to leave unspoken." (Ch. 1)
"In the beginning the word was largely a pass-word, granting admission to a nucleus of like speakers." (Ch. 3)
"Streaming outward it thins, losing energy and pressure as it reaches an alien speaker." (Ch. 3)
fields.Themes: privacy of language, hermeticism, concealment, pass-word, linguistic exogamy, hermeneutic motion, borrowing concordance

fields.Title: 'Insubordinate Irish': Travellers in the Text
fields.Author: Mícheál Ó hAodha
fields.Role_in_Set: Oblique edge: Shelta as a living private core, likely formed in the same Irish-to-English shift; its outside 'discoverers' as the philologist's counterpart to the sappers
fields.Selection_Logic: Gives the Victorian origin myths of Shelta and the modern view that it was formed during the language shift; shows outsiders valuing a hidden tongue only for antiquity and reading concealment as degeneracy.
fields.Quotes:
"most scholars who have examined Shelta are now of the opinion that Shelta was formed in the modern period, possibly at that juncture when the language shift from Irish to English was taking place" (p. 18)
"I would scarcely have taken much interest in Shelta, if it were nothing but tinkers’ cant, fabricated from Irish in modern times, of a kind not superior to the backslang of costers and cabmen." (Meyer, quoted p. 21)
"moral and social code, like his language, is certainly of the backslang order" (Sampson, quoted p. 21)
"the most curious linguistic discovery of the century, the fifth British Celtic tongue!" (Leland, quoted p. 17)
"the subaltern or ‘Other’ is represented and ‘translated’ through the essentialist language of the dominant culture" (p. 56)
"They break into this when unwilling to be heard at their business." (IFC respondent, p. 89)
fields.Themes: Shelta, Gammon, Cant, Gypsy Lore Society, Tinker Questionnaire, anti-language, road-signs, origin myths, language shift

fields.Title: The Last Days of Mankind: The Complete Text
fields.Author: Karl Kraus (trans. Fred Bridgham and Edward Timms)
fields.Role_in_Set: Ancestor: the documentary method with a commentator (the Grumbler); source of the participle Bäcker's note cites.
fields.Selection_Logic: First large work built on the claim that ordered quotations accuse their speakers; its Preface disclaims invention; its Przemysl pair shows composition by reversal alone; the Grumbler is the voice Bäcker refuses.
fields.Quotes:
"The most improbable conversations conducted here were spoken word for word; the most lurid fantasies are quotations." (Preface)
"The document takes human shape; reports come alive as characters and characters expire as editorials; the newspaper column has acquired a mouth that spouts monologues; platitudes stand on two legs—unlike men left with only one." (Preface)
"Universal conscription has turned mankind into a passive noun. Once men joined the forces, now they’re forced to join." (II, 10)
"Thanks for the compliment, but don’t you remember? My most lurid fantasies are quotations!" (V, 44)
"Not by hunger but by enemy action—damn, what am I saying—not by enemy action but by hunger!" (II, 16) / "Not by force but by hunger—dammit, what am I saying! Not by hunger but by force!" (III, 22)
fields.Themes: satire, quotation, Die Fackel, press, war, Grumbler, Optimist, passive participle, compulsorily enlisted, Przemysl, montage

fields.Title: Transcript
fields.Author: Heimrad Bäcker (trans. Patrick Greaney and Vincent Kling; ed. Friedrich Achleitner)
fields.Role_in_Set: Center: the documentary method with no commentator; cites Kraus in its own notes.
fields.Selection_Logic: Does what Kraus's Preface claims, without a Grumbler: Nazi documents isolated on blank pages by the methods of concrete poetry; argues against 'unspeakability'. Internet Archive OCR scan; quotations checked against the OCR layer.
fields.Quotes:
"Every part of transcript is a quotation; anything that might seem invented or fantastic is a verifiable document. Slight changes and omissions (which allow the unaltered contents to stand out in sharper relief) are not explicitly indicated." (notes headnote, p. 131)
"...sometimes to the point of a methodical gibberish that replicates a deadly gibberish." (p. 131)
"Himmler’s language reflects the progressive logic of the system: in 1942 being emigrated meant to be destroyed." (note 16, p. 132)
"Documents are literature that writes itself and is recognized as literature." (Bäcker in Achleitner's afterword, p. 148)
"the card file on the dead was larger by far than the one on the living." (p. 127)
fields.Themes: documentary poetry, concrete poetry, Holocaust, Nazi bureaucratic language, quotation, permutation, lists, being emigrated, ineffability, Vienna Group

fields.Title: Mornings Like This
fields.Author: Annie Dillard
fields.Role_in_Set: Control case: same method (omission, never addition) producing delight instead of indictment.
fields.Selection_Logic: Found poems from old manuals, memoirs and textbooks; the Author's Note states the vow ('I never added a word') and the cost ('the original authors’ intentions were usually first to go'), the exact opposite of Bäcker's use.
fields.Quotes:
"By entering a found text as a poem, the poet doubles its context. The original meaning remains intact, but now it swings between two poles." (Author's Note)
"In the course of composing such found poems, the original authors’ intentions were usually first to go." (Author's Note)
"Sometimes I dropped extra words; I never added a word." (Author's Note)
"This is editing at its extreme: writing without composing." (Author's Note)
"Stop carrying out your intentions." (Signals at Sea, poem 16)
fields.Themes: found poetry, omission, delight, intention, manuals, last words, signals, Picard, Ellsworth Kelly

fields.Title: Religio Medici and Urne-Buriall
fields.Author: Sir Thomas Browne
fields.Role_in_Set: Hinge: holds both Russian positions at once — faith that scattered ashes reassemble (God's work) and scepticism toward every human preservation; mummy ends on the apothecary's shelf.
fields.Selection_Logic: Religio Medici I.47–48 states resurrection of divided dust and supports it by palingenesis (plant revived from its ashes); Urne-Buriall V catalogues the failures of pyramids, mummies, inscriptions; uses 'Ossuaries' (1658). Years: RM 1642/43, UB 1658; NYRB ed. 2012.
fields.Quotes: "I beleeve that our estranged and divided ashes shall unite againe; that our separated dust after so many pilgrimages and transformations into the parts of mineralls, Plants, Animals, Elements, shall at the voyce of God returne into their primitive shapes, and joyne againe to make up their primary and predestinated formes." (RM I.48) | "I have heard some with deepe sighs lament the lost lines of Cicero; others with as many groanes deplore the combustion of the Library of Alexandria; for my owne part, I thinke there be too many in the world, and could with patience behold the urne and ashes of the Vatican" (RM I.24) | "But who knows the fate of his bones, or how often he is to be buried? who hath the Oracle of his ashes, or whither they are to be scattered?" (UB, Epistle Dedicatory) | "He that hath the ashes of his friend, hath an everlasting treasure" (UB III) | "But the iniquity of oblivion blindely scattereth her poppy, and deals with the memory of men without distinction to merit of perpetuity." (UB V) | "The Ægyptian Mummies, which Cambyses or time hath spared, avarice now consumeth. Mummie is become Merchandise, Miszraim cures wounds, and Pharaoh is sold for balsoms." (UB V) | "Though the earth had confounded the ashes of these Ossuaries, yet the bones were so smartly burnt, that some thin plates of brasse were found half melted among them" (UB III)
fields.Themes: ashes, resurrection, palingenesis, urn burial, ossuary, mummy, apothecary, oblivion, monuments, antiquarianism

fields.Title: Russian Cosmism
fields.Author: Boris Groys (ed.)
fields.Role_in_Set: The resurrection programme: Fedorov removes Browne's deferral to God and gives the work to art/biology; Groys makes the museum the machine of immortality; Bogdanov's 'Immortality Day' ends on a pyre.
fields.Selection_Logic: Groys's Introduction ('Russian Cosmism and the Technology of Immortality') states the museum-as-immortality thesis Malevich attacks; Fedorov's 'Astronomy and Architecture' (Earth as cemetery, art as resurrection, contempt for portrait-substitutes); Svyatogor demotes resurrection; Bogdanov's immortal Fride chooses the stake. Edition MIT/e-flux 2018; texts c.1880s–1920s.
fields.Quotes: "The museum, by contrast, is a machine for making things last, making them immortal." (Groys, Introduction) | "And the state must become the museum of its population." (Groys, Introduction) | "Art, if it is the work of a rational being, must consist precisely in the resurrection of everything destroyed by blind force" (Fedorov, 'Astronomy and Architecture') | "For the arts (sculpture, painting) offer but to replace those bodies destroyed, with stone, with metal, with figurations not easily effaced" (Fedorov, 'Astronomy and Architecture') | "Being a cemetery, the Earth holds within it as many generations as there are worlds in the universe not ruled by reason" (Fedorov, 'Astronomy and Architecture') | "with resurrection being relegated to third place" (Svyatogor, 'The Doctrine of the Fathers and Anarchism-Biocosmism') | "“To burn at the stake! At the very least, it will be beautiful.”" (Bogdanov, 'Immortality Day', §6) | "Tongues of fire twisted around his body, hissing: “Everything repeats itself!”" (Bogdanov, 'Immortality Day', §6)
fields.Themes: Russian Cosmism, Fedorov, common task, resurrection, museum as immortality, biopower, Biocosmism, Bogdanov, immortality, pyre

fields.Title: Avant-Garde Museology
fields.Author: Arseny Zhilyaev (ed.)
fields.Role_in_Set: The counter-position and its institutional sequel: Malevich's 'On the Museum' (1919) — the dead as powder on one chemist's shelf — and Levitsky's 1931 review of a crematorium exhibition.
fields.Selection_Logic: Prints Fedorov's 'The Museum, its Meaning and Mission' (Part I) beside Malevich (Part II) and the Atheists' Museum section (Part VI); word-frequency by part shows resurrect-/dead vanish after Part I and cremat- peaks in Part VI. Printed page = PDF page − 1.
fields.Quotes: "Contemporary life has invented crematoria for the dead, but each dead man is more alive than a weakly painted portrait. In burning a corpse we obtain one gram of powder: accordingly, thousands of graveyards could be accommodated on one chemist’s shelf." (Malevich, p. 270) | "Our contemporary life should have as its slogan: “all that we have made is made for the crematorium.”" (Malevich, p. 270) | "enough pawning the graveyards of Vagankovo, enough singing requiems—none of this will rise again." (Malevich, p. 270) | "Our job is not to photograph remains—that is what photographs are for." (Malevich, p. 272) | "A museum, we could say, is a cemetery that has been transported and placed in the center of the city" (Fedorov, p. 132) | "Is cremation at all necessary, or is it better to abide by the age-old custom of burying the dead?" (Levitsky, p. 555) | "This is not just a technical error, but a crude ideological blunder on the part of the exhibition’s organizers." (Levitsky, p. 556)
fields.Themes: Malevich, museum, crematorium, cremation, pharmacy, avant-garde, Soviet museology, antireligious museum, Fedorov, Levitsky, Bekhterev

fields.Title: Gesture and Speech
fields.Author: André Leroi-Gourhan (trans. Anna Bostock Berger; intro. Randall White)
fields.Role_in_Set: The source: graphism begins as rhythmic, abstract incision; writing linearizes it into a 'needle-sharp, but also needle-thin' line; the Jacquard loom exteriorizes the program.
fields.Selection_Logic: Ingold builds the close of his writing chapter on it; supplies the triad's deepest claim (abstraction and the rhythmic incised line come first). Printed page = PDF page − 20 in the 'Language Symbols' chapters.
fields.Quotes: "They take the form of tight curves or series of lines engraved in bone or stone, small equidistant incisions that provide evidence of figurative representation moving away from the concretely figurative and proof of the earliest rhythmic manifestations." (p. 188) | "If there is one point of which we may be absolutely sure, it is that graphism did not begin with naive representations of reality but with abstraction." (p. 188) | "Four thousand years of linear writing have accustomed us to separating art from writing" (p. 192) | "... a cosmos whose center they occupy without trying to pierce it by an intellectual process which letters have strung out in a needle-sharp, but also needle-thin, line." (p. 200) | "The gesture interprets the word, and the word comments upon graphic expression." (p. 210) | "Written language, phoneticized and linear in space, becomes completely subordinated to spoken language, which is phonetic and linear in time." (p. 210) | "The program of the Jacquard loom is external to the organs of execution" (p. 250)
fields.Themes: graphism, linearization, rhythm, incision, abstraction, mythogram, picto-ideography, exteriorization, Jacquard loom, gesture

fields.Title: Lines: A Brief History
fields.Author: Tim Ingold
fields.Role_in_Set: The hinge: inherits Leroi-Gourhan's linearization thesis, names its paradox, and traces the ruled line back to the warp-thread of the loom.
fields.Selection_Logic: Explicit genealogy from Leroi-Gourhan (ch. 5) plus the material history (masara, ruler as sovereign, no drawn line perfectly straight) that reaches Martin's studio. Printed page = PDF page − 13.
fields.Quotes: "Fully linearized, the line is no longer the trace of a gesture but a chain of point-to-point connections. In these connections there is neither life nor movement. Linearization, in short, marks not the birth but the death of the line." (ch. 5, p. 151) | "For Semper the prototypical line was a thread; for Riegl it was a trace" (ch. 2, p. 42) | "more like a series of appointments than a walk" (Klee, quoted ch. 3, p. 73) | "the straight lines of the ruled manuscript, which guided the writer’s hand in weaving the letter-line, can be traced back to the parallel warp-threads of the loom. The threads were straight because they were taut." (ch. 6, p. 157) | "A ruler is a sovereign who controls and governs a territory. It is also an instrument for drawing straight lines." (p. 160) | "Only when the architect ceased to be a master-builder and retreated to the drawingboard were templates replaced by the ruler, and taut threads by the ruled traces of the diagram." (p. 161) | "so no line that is ever drawn – even with a ruler – can ever be perfectly straight. An element of risk is always involved." (p. 162)
fields.Themes: line, thread, trace, ghostly line, ruled line, ruler, loom, warp, masara, wayfaring, linearization, Klee, Semper, Riegl, Ruskin, Pye

fields.Title: Agnes Martin: Night Sea
fields.Author: Suzanne P. Hudson
fields.Role_in_Set: The test case: a grid of scored, gilded lines ruled with threads from Tawney's loom; the 'visual tremolo' as Ingold's risk; after 1963 Martin linearizes her own practice.
fields.Selection_Logic: Material evidence for both theories in one painting; its lines fall under all four of Ingold's classes (thread, trace, cut, ghostly). Printed page = PDF page − 1.
fields.Quotes: "scored and sometimes gilded, they generate pattern in and as surface." (p. 13) | "the six-foot span – Martin’s standard canvas size as of 1960 – measures the reach of her own arms." (p. 16) | "Near the top right corner, the main lines veer off track to the right, and the horizontal bands dip ever so slightly. The slopes show how her implementation of markings was keyed to her movement." (p. 16) | "Accident betrays her." (p. 17) | "these marks positively evidence what Annette Michelson once characterised as a distinctively human ‘visual tremolo’, which is to say, that they are aleatory and minutely flawed." (p. 17) | "she could not conceal the journey of her hand across the page, or the systems she put in place to attempt regulation." (p. 18) | "in addition to a T-square and ruler, Martin used threads to track vertical and horizontal coordinates, a trick assimilated from watching Tawney dress her loom" (Sachs, quoted p. 36) | "Well, when I first made a grid I happened to be thinking of the innocence of trees" (Martin, quoted p. 45)
fields.Themes: Agnes Martin, Night Sea, grid, visual tremolo, Lenore Tawney, Coenties Slip, loom, threads, scored line, classicism, process, Krauss

fields.Title: Sabbatai Ṣevi: The Mystical Messiah, 1626-1676
fields.Author: Gershom Scholem (trans. R. J. Zwi Werblowsky)
fields.Role_in_Set: The anchor and the historian's case: three disconfirmations (imprisonment, apostasy, death) each turned into doctrine; explicit parallel with Paul and early Christianity.
fields.Selection_Logic: The best-documented case of a faith surviving refutation of its central claim; Scholem himself invokes Renan and Paul, which brings in Schweitzer. Duplicate record: 5724. Hebrew 1957; English 1973; Princeton Classics 2016. Pages are print pages embedded in the EPUB.
fields.Quotes: "To believe in an apostate messiah was to build one’s hope on foundations of paradox and absurdity, which could only lead to more paradoxes." (p. 690) | "The Sabbatian paradox, however, was not that of a saint who suffers and whose suffering is a mystery hidden with God, but of a saint who sins." (p. 691) | "adopt the dress of the people through whose land he passes, and to behave as they do, lest they notice that he is a spy" (p. 802) | "Readers of Paul’s letters can learn a great deal from these later Jewish writings, composed in a very similar psychological situation." (p. 803) | "And finally he [that is, the messiah] will restore [to holiness] his qelippah which is Jesus Christ." (p. 285) | "Neither Our Lord nor anything else was in the cave, but it was full of light." (p. 920) | "Return every man to his house. How long will you hold fast to me?" (p. 917) | "Enthusiasm and love know of no hopeless situations. They play with the impossible, and rather than despair, they violate reality." (Renan, quoted p. 689)
fields.Themes: Sabbatianism, apostasy, Nathan of Gaza, occultation, holy ruse, qelippah, tiqqun, paradox, Paul, Renan, Dulcigno

fields.Title: The Quest of the Historical Jesus
fields.Author: Albert Schweitzer (trans. W. Montgomery)
fields.Role_in_Set: The theologian's case and genealogical middle term: Christianity as the history of the delay of the Parousia; Reimarus's stolen body; Renan's novelistic Life.
fields.Selection_Logic: Thoroughgoing eschatology puts a failed prophecy at the origin of a religion, the structure Scholem sees again in 1666; its Renan chapter links to both Scholem and the novel. Dover EPUB, no print pagination; located by chapter.
fields.Quotes: "The whole history of “ Christianity ” down to the present day, that is to say, the real inner history of it, is based on the delay of the Parousia, the non-occurrence of the Parousia" (ch. XIX) | "lays hold of the wheel of the world to set it moving on that last revolution which is to bring all ordinary history to a close" (ch. XIX) | "So they stole the body of Jesus and hid it, and proclaimed to all the world that He would soon return." (ch. II) | "Accordingly, the main problem of primitive dogmatics was the delay of the Parousia." (ch. II) | "There is no historical task which so reveals a man’s true self as the writing of a Life of Jesus." (ch. I) | "He planned the work at Gaza" (ch. XIII, on Renan)
fields.Themes: eschatology, Parousia, delay, de-eschatologizing, Reimarus, Renan, lives of Jesus, Paul, apocalyptic prophet

fields.Title: The Coming
fields.Author: Andrej Nikolaidis (trans. Will Firth)
fields.Role_in_Set: The novelist's case: a noir in Ulcinj where Sabbatai's followers burn books so he can return; the non-occurrence of the End as the catastrophe.
fields.Selection_Logic: Fiction set in Sabbatai's exile town that can be checked line by line against Scholem (birth, exile, death date, last words); Kafka epigraph and Dr Schulz's catalogue of failed Ends. Montenegrin Dolazak 2009; English © 2011 (Dzanc).
fields.Quotes: "The non-occurrence of the catastrophe was a catastrophe which ultimately made the world impossible to live in." (ch. 9) | "Truth always appears as a fiction and takes the form of a story. I am a storyteller." (ch. 1) | "The third was now dug out of its tomb: the Messiah could come again." (ch. 6) | "He died in Ulcinj on 30 September 1676. That was Yom Kippur." (ch. 6) | "When a good sleuth and God are finished, no further interpretation is possible, there’s only applause" (ch. 8) | "The Apocalypse had been a kind of solution, after all." (ch. 9) | "The Messiah will come only when he is no longer necessary; he will come only on the day after his arrival" (Kafka, epigraph)
fields.Themes: apocalypse, failed end-dates, Sabbatai Zevi, Ulcinj, Fra Dolcino, Dönme, book burning, detective fiction, storytelling, fathers and sons, Kafka

fields.Title: In the Dark Places of Wisdom
fields.Author: Peter Kingsley
fields.Role_in_Set: Anchor: the sacred, literal sense of incubation and the supervisor figure
fields.Selection_Logic: Supplies the older sense of 'incubation' (lying down in a lair, waiting without effort) and the priest 'in charge of the place'; without it Wallas's word reads as neutral metaphor.
fields.Quotes:
"What's important is that you would do absolutely nothing. The point came when you wouldn't struggle or make an effort. You'd just have to surrender to your condition." (p. 80)
"It's all tied up with that clumsy word: incubation." (p. 101)
"Usually you'd lie down in a special place where you wouldn't be disturbed." (p. 101)
"It used to mean giving a voice to what doesn't have a voice, meant acting as a mouthpiece for the divine." (p. 108)
"Really it was already the end itself, the ultimate paradox of the end that's present at the beginning." (p. 186)
fields.Themes: incubation, lair, phōleos, Phōlarchos, hesychia, stillness, iatromantis, Parmenides, Velia, Apollo

fields.Title: The Art of Thought
fields.Author: Graham Wallas
fields.Role_in_Set: Hinge: secularizes incubation and illumination as stages of thought; states the observation problem (corona/eclipse)
fields.Selection_Logic: Where 'incubation' and 'illumination' enter the modern vocabulary of creativity without the cult behind them. Scanned PDF with no text layer: chapter IV OCR'd with tesseract; quotes from that OCR, PDF page locations.
fields.Quotes:
"it is desirable not only that there should be an interval free from conscious thought on the particular problem concerned, but also that that interval should be so spent that nothing should interfere with the free working of the unconscious or partially conscious processes of the mind. In those cases, the stage of Incubation should include a large amount of actual mental relaxation." (ch. IV, PDF p. 103)
"Even in exploring the same problem, the mind may be unconsciously incubating on one aspect of it, while it is consciously employed in preparing for or verifying another aspect." (PDF p. 97)
"And yet a thinker of good health and naturally fertile mind may have to be told that mere industry is for him, as it was for Trollope in his later years, the worst temptation of the devil." (PDF p. 104)
"in that periphery or 'fringe' of consciousness which surrounds our 'focal' consciousness as the sun's 'corona' surrounds the disk of full luminosity." (PDF p. 111)
"Each was followed by a period of Verification, in which both the validity of the idea was tested, and the idea itself was reduced to exact form." (PDF p. 96)
fields.Themes: Preparation, Incubation, Illumination, Verification, Intimation, fringe consciousness, Helmholtz, Poincaré, mental relaxation, industry

fields.Title: On Hashish
fields.Author: Walter Benjamin (ed./trans. Howard Eiland; intro. Marcus Boon)
fields.Role_in_Set: Counter-voice: keeps the posture and the word illumination, makes it profane; the protocol with a hole in it
fields.Selection_Logic: Benjamin lies down and waits with a physician keeping the record, and argues the source of illumination is profane. Fränkel's protocol, broken off when note-taking is forbidden, is the best evidence for the observation problem.
fields.Quotes:
"the second of these secrets cannot be recovered, since at this point the compiler of the protocol was very energetically prohibited from taking notes." (Fränkel protocol, Apr. 18, 1931, p. 77)
"I lay on my bed, read, and smoked." ('Myslovice—Braunschweig—Marseilles', p. 110)
"LYING DOWN, with eyes closed most of the time, completely calm." (Wissing protocol, Mar. 7, 1931, p. 65)
"But the true, creative overcoming of religious illumination certainly does not lie in narcotics. It resides in a profane illumination, a materialistic, anthropological inspiration" ('Surrealism', p. 132)
"Just as waiting seems to be the proper state of the impassive thinker, doubt appears to be that of the flaneur." (Arcades M2,4, p. 139)
"The reader, the thinker, the person who waits, the flaneur, are types of illuminati—just as much as the opium eater, the dreamer, the ecstatic. And more profane." (p. 134)
fields.Themes: protocols, profane illumination, hashish, waiting, note-taking, Fränkel, Joël, Wissing, Surrealism, flaneur

fields.Title: The Ghost Rider
fields.Author: Ismail Kadare (trans. Jon Rothschild, rev. David Bellos)
fields.Role_in_Set: Anchor: the oath as a social institution; a besa kept by a dead man, raised by his mother's curse
fields.Selection_Logic: The only fiction of the three that treats the oath as an institution rather than a plot device: the besa is debated like a constitution (ch. 6) and given a resurrection (ch. 7). Captain Stres's search for a living impostor gives the triad its rationalist resistance. Bellos's introduction ties the ballad to Bürger's 'Lenore'.
fields.Quotes:
“So who did Bürger steal it from?” the young woman asks. (Introduction, David Bellos)
‘Now I am left alone in the world, for you have broken your promise. May the earth never receive you!’ (ch. 2)
A curse be on thee, Kostandin! Do you recall the solemn promise you made? Or has your besa rotted with you in the grave? (ch. 3)
It was still very rare: delicate, like a wild flower needing tender care, its shape as yet undefined. (ch. 6)
Except for one thing, Captain Stres: there was no default. He kept his promise in the end. (ch. 6)
Therefore, to be more exact I would have to say that it was all of us – you, me, our dead lying there in the graveyard close by the church – who, through Kostandin, brought Doruntine back. (ch. 7)
fields.Themes: besa, curse, promise beyond death, revenant, dead rider, Albanian ballad, kanun, Stres, rationalism vs legend

fields.Title: The Omnibus Homo Sacer ('The Sacrament of Language: An Archaeology of the Oath')
fields.Author: Giorgio Agamben (trans. Adam Kotsko)
fields.Role_in_Set: Theory and hinge: oath = affirmation + witness + curse; blessing and curse co-originary; magic born from perjury
fields.Selection_Logic: Turns a folk motif and its descendants into two dramatizations of one structure: the oath binds the speaker's life to his word, and the curse is that binding when the word fails. It explains why the mother's curse can do what it does in Kadare and why the vampire's 'Remember your oath' works as a gag.
fields.Quotes:
"The oath does not in any way constitute a remedy against the “Indo-European scourge”; instead, the scourge itself is contained within it in the form of perjury." (p. 306 / PDF 315)
"The oath seems, then, to result from the conjunction of three elements: an affirmation, the invocation of the gods as witnesses, and a curse directed at perjury." (p. 324 / PDF 333)
"The name of the god, which signifies and guarantees the juncture between words and things, is transformed into a curse if this relation is broken. What is essential, in every case, is the co-originarity of blessing and curse, which are constitutively copresent in the oath." (p. 328 / PDF 337)
"The oath is not a conditional curse: on the contrary, the curse and its symmetrical pendant, the blessing, are born as specific institutions from the division of the experience of speech that was in question in the oath." (p. 333 / PDF 342)
"It is from the oath—or, better, from perjury—that magic and spells are born: the formula of truth, when broken, is transformed into an efficacious curse" (p. 333 / PDF 342)
"law and religion are born, both of which seek to tie speech to things and to bind, by means of curses and anathemas, speaking subjects to the veritative power of their speech" (p. 345 / PDF 354)
"Every naming is, in fact, double: it is a blessing or a curse." (p. 353 / PDF 362)
"Precisely because, unlike other living things, in order to speak, the human being must put himself at stake in his speech, he can, for this reason, bless and curse, swear and perjure." (p. 355 / PDF 364)
fields.Themes: oath, curse, perjury, horkos, epiorkos, ara, sacratio, fides, bene-diction, male-diction, anathema, sacrament of power, technicalization

fields.Title: Vampyres: Genesis and Resurrection, from Count Dracula to Vampirella
fields.Author: Christopher Frayling (ed.)
fields.Role_in_Set: Genealogy and inversion: Lenore → 'the dead travel fast'; the vampire tale opens with an extracted oath that silences the living
fields.Selection_Logic: Supplies the line of descent from the ballad (Bürger's 'Lenore' quoted in Dracula ch. 1; Frayling's note on its removal from the Munich section) and the primary texts where the oath is the vampire's first tool: Byron's 'Fragment', Polidori, and the self-cursing ballad in Tolstoy's 'Vourdalak'. Polidori's Aubrey is Kostandin inverted.
fields.Quotes:
‘Swear by all your soul reveres, by all your nature fears, swear that for a year and a day you will not impart your knowledge of my crimes or death to any living being in any way, whatever may happen, or whatever you may see.’ (Polidori, The Vampyre; Part Two §2)
‘Remember your oath, and know, if not my bride today, your sister is dishonoured. Women are frail!’ (Polidori; Part Two §2)
‘Swear it, by all that – ’ He here dictated an oath of great solemnity. (Byron, 'Fragment of a Story'; Part Two §2)
‘I swear to be faithful to you and never to forget you. If I should break my oath, come to me after your death and drink all my heart’s blood!’ (A. K. Tolstoy, 'The Family of the Vourdalak'; Part Two §4)
One of my companions whispered to another the line from Burger’s ‘Lenore’: – Denn die Todten reiten schnell – (For the dead travel fast.) (Stoker, Dracula ch. 1; Part Two §6)
The quotation ‘the dead travel fast’ (from Bürger’s poem Lenore ) was at some stage removed from the Munich section of the novel (Frayling, headnote to §6)
fields.Themes: vampire genealogy, Lenore, the dead travel fast, Polidori, Ruthven, Aubrey, oath as gag, Byron's Fragment, Vourdalak, Dracula's Guest, Stoker's working papers

fields.Title: Life: A User's Manual
fields.Author: Georges Perec (trans. David Bellos)
fields.Role_in_Set: Anchor: the graph narrated from inside — a building walked one room per chapter; the Preamble states the relational premise.
fields.Selection_Logic: The jigsaw Preamble ('the pattern determines the parts') is structuralism in a puzzle-maker's voice; the novel stages it as 99 chapters over 100 squares (knight's tour, unstated in the text) and ends with a piece that cannot fit (W vs X). Its own contents yield the walk: Stairs 12 chapters, 36 locations.
fields.Quotes:
“the parts do not determine the pattern, but the pattern determines the parts” (Preamble)
“The eye follows the paths that have been laid down for it in the work (Paul Klee, Pädagogisches Skizzenbuch )” (Preamble epigraph)
“a vertical cross-section of the building giving a diagrammatic picture of the layout of the flats” (Ch. 1)
“an arbitrarily constrained programme with no purpose outside its own completion” (Ch. 26)
“the black hole of the sole piece not yet filled in has the almost perfect shape of an X. But the ironical thing, which could have been foreseen long ago, is that the piece the dead man holds between his fingers is shaped like a W.” (Ch. 99)
“dividing it up into regular square boxes, the sketch of a cross-section of a block of flats which no figure, now, would ever come to inhabit.” (Epilogue)
“in isolation, a puzzle piece means nothing – just an impossible question, an opaque challenge.” (Preamble)
fields.Themes: jigsaw, Gestalt, pattern vs parts, cross-section, knight's tour, hamiltonian path, Oulipo, Bartlebooth, Valène, stairwell as hub, missing square

fields.Title: Network Theory, Plot Analysis (Literary Lab Pamphlet 2)
fields.Author: Franco Moretti
fields.Role_in_Set: Experiment: turns Hamlet into a network and removes vertices; position, not essence, makes Horatio indispensable.
fields.Selection_Logic: Applies the relational premise to a canonical play and tests it by deletion: Hamlet removed splits the network; Claudius removed changes little (clustering); Hamlet + Horatio removed severs Ghost and Fortinbras. Also the conflict pole: works by hand, admits lacking the mathematics.
fields.Quotes:
“A network is made of vertices and edges; a plot, of characters and actions: characters will be the vertices of the network, interactions the edges” (p. 3)
“two characters are linked if some words have passed between them: an interaction, is a speech act.” (p. 3)
“Anyway. Four hours of action, that become this. Time turned into space” (p. 3)
“what is truly deadly, is the characters’ position in the network, chained to the warring poles of king and prince. Outside of that red region, no one dies in Hamlet. The tragedy, is all there.” (p. 4)
“Not for what is “in” it; not for its essence, but for its function in the stability of the network.” (p. 5)
“Horatio has a function in the play, but not a motivation.” (p. 7)
“The theory proper requires a level of mathematical intelligence which I unfortunately lack” (p. 2)
fields.Themes: character network, Hamlet, Horatio, removal experiment, centrality, average distance, clustering, weak tie, power law, region of death, time into space, distant reading

fields.Title: Structural Models in Anthropology
fields.Author: Per Hage & Frank Harary
fields.Role_in_Set: Formal ground: exact definitions (cutpoint, bridge, hamiltonian, eulerian) and the claim that graph theory is already in anthropology.
fields.Selection_Logic: Gives the vocabulary Moretti uses by eye and the best parallel for Perec's hidden structure: New Hebrides sand drawings, which practise Euler's theorem (one line, finger never lifted) without stating it. Insists the mathematics must be made explicit.
fields.Quotes:
“But classification according to structure is generally more important. And it is the same with ideas.” (epigraph, Peirce)
“In theory the whole should be done in a single continuous line which ends where it began; the finger should never be lifted from the ground, nor should any part of the line be traversed twice” (p. 10, quoting Deacon 1934)
“whatever the particular configurations may look like or represent, they are eulerian; that is, they are connected and all points have even degree.” (p. 12)
“Euler replaced each land area by a point and each bridge by a line joining the corresponding points, thereby producing the first published graph theoretic model.” (p. 12)
“graph theory is such a congenial mode of anthropological thought that if Euler had not discovered it, some anthropologist might very well have.” (p. 13)
“A cutpoint of a connected graph is one whose removal (together with its incident lines) disconnects it” (p. 19)
“If a graph G has a spanning cycle Z, then G is called a hamiltonian graph and Z is a hamiltonian cycle.” (p. 26)
“the individuals and relations represented by cutpoints and bridges would presumably be of fundamental importance in the group.” (p. 29)
fields.Themes: graph theory, structural anthropology, Euler, Königsberg, sand drawings, eulerian, hamiltonian, cutpoint, bridge, Lévi-Strauss, Klein group, Peirce, implicit mathematics

fields.Title: The Conscience of Words (with Earwitness)
fields.Author: Elias Canetti
fields.Role_in_Set: Day 1 primary: the author's own work, standing in for Crowds and Power (not yet in the catalogue).

“But the crucial moment is the moment of the sultan’s onlyness” (p. 24)

“Whole constellations dissolved” (p. 26)

fields.Title: The Travels of Ibn Battuta: In the Near East, Asia and Africa, 1325-1354
fields.Author: Ibn Battuta (tr. Samuel Lee)
fields.Role_in_Set: Source check: Canetti's named source for the Delhi story; chapter XVI read and set against Canetti's retelling.
fields.Selection_Logic: Canetti insists the sultan's line 'is not a later invention or embroidery' and names Ibn Batuta as his source; the library holds Lee's abridged translation.
fields.Quotes:
“which is at the distance of ten days” (ch. XVI)
“only one of his legs was brought to the place intended” (ch. XVI)
“When I entered Dehli it was almost a desert.” (ch. XVI)
“the greatest city in the world had the fewest inhabitants.” (ch. XVI)
fields.Themes: Muhammad Tughluq; Delhi; Daulatabad; sources; abridgement

fields.Title: Dostoyevsky Reads Hegel in Siberia and Bursts Into Tears
fields.Author: László F. Földényi (tr. Ottilie Mulzet)
fields.Role_in_Set: Day 2 primary (quotes): 'A Capacity for Amazement: Canetti's Crowds and Power Fifty Years Later' and 'Mass and Spirit'.
fields.Selection_Logic: Second only to the Companion (3312) in a scan of the 330 non-own Mentions books: 87 'Canetti', 32 'Crowds and Power'; an essayist quoting an essayist, with page-cited quotations checkable against the Stewart translation (14938).
fields.Quotes:
“Elias Canetti’s book is strictly speaking not a novel, although there is something very novel-like in its texture.” (A Capacity for Amazement)
“His citation apparatus, for example, is, to put it mildly, unusual.” (ibid.)
“Canetti never employs the first-person singular, and yet his book is deeply personal.” (ibid.)
“I have often thought that this is the most important book I know.” (ibid., n. 1)
“For my own part, I would not compare his work with that of Hannah Arendt, but with Kafka’s.” (ibid.)
“Under Canetti’s gaze, the crowd becomes an organism, a beast that crouches under the phenomena of world history. The result is a sort of mystical primitivism.” (Rothstein, quoted ibid., n. 9)
fields.Themes: Crowds and Power; Hegel and Africa; first person; retranslation; myth; command; vision

fields.Title: A Temple of Texts
fields.Author: William H. Gass
fields.Year: 2006 (essays; 'The Road to the True Book' first in The New Republic, Nov. 1982, revised)
fields.Role_in_Set: Day 2 primary (quotes): 'The Road to the True Book' (on the memoirs) and 'Influence' (Palace of Justice, Büchner, Brand/Kant/Kien).
fields.Selection_Logic: 83 'Canetti'; two essays quoting the memoirs and The Conscience of Words at length, all checkable against 413, 418, 420, 421.
fields.Quotes:
“Then the word I—that moist reedlike letter that makes the winds sing, that wonderful word for me—takes ten typical bows in our specimen paragraph” (The Road to the True Book)
“Well … to remember is to give limbs to a new lie.” (ibid.)
“Canetti’s tact with time and knowledge is one of the artistic triumphs of these memoirs.” (ibid.)
“A deceased Nobel laureate, Elias Canetti has now achieved such fame as to be unknown all over the world.” (ibid.)
“Moreover, after at first naming the character Kant, he called him Kien, meaning ‘kindling,’ so what was possible for that person but ignition?” (Influence)
“and in the shooting and its subsequent panic, ninety people were killed and many more injured.” (Influence)
fields.Themes: autobiography; memory; noise; naming; Palace of Justice fire; Büchner; revision

fields.Title: Crowds and Power
fields.Author: Elias Canetti (tr. Carol Stewart)
fields.Role_in_Set: Source check for Földényi's quotations and his first-person claim (not read as a primary).
fields.Selection_Logic: Added to the catalogue 2026-10-26; the target of Földényi's notes 2–3, 8, 10, 12–14.
fields.Quotes:
“It is not for a European of the 20th century to regard himself as above savagery. His despots may use more effective means, but their ends often differ in nothing from those of these African Kings.” (Rulers and Paranoiacs: African Kings)
“I am here deliberately opposing all the usual concepts of tribe, sib, clan” (The Pack)
“I use the same word ‘pack’ for the three other basic formations I have mentioned.” (The Pack)
“We must have the courage to stand against it and break its tyranny.” (The Command)
fields.Themes: crowd; pack; command; African kings; first person

fields.Title: The Torch in My Ear
fields.Author: Elias Canetti
fields.Role_in_Set: Source check for Gass's block quotations.
fields.Selection_Logic: Source of 'I bow to memory', the mother's accusation, and 'the road to the true book'.
fields.Quotes:
“I bow to memory, every person’s memory.” (ch. Escape)
“I had barely set out on the road to the true book: each individual human being, bound in himself.” (The Letters in the Tree)
“even transplant hearts that manage to beat along for another year” (Escape)
fields.Themes: memory; autobiography

fields.Title: The Play of the Eyes
fields.Author: Elias Canetti (tr. Ralph Manheim)
fields.Role_in_Set: Source check for Gass's 'Influence' (Büchner night).
fields.Selection_Logic: Gass quotes 'Büchner in the Desert' at length.
fields.Quotes:
“which had long been on my shelf but which I had never touched.” (Büchner in the Desert)
“My novel that I’d been so proud of crumbled into dust and ashes.” (ibid.)
fields.Themes: Büchner; Lenz; Woyzeck; delayed encounter

fields.Title: The Tongue Set Free
fields.Author: Elias Canetti
fields.Role_in_Set: Source check for Gass (the knife and the tongue).
fields.Selection_Logic: Gass opens his account of the memoirs with 'My Earliest Memory'.
fields.Quotes: “The threat with the knife worked, the child quite literally held his tongue for ten years.” (My Earliest Memory)
fields.Themes: tongue; silence; earliest memory

fields.Title: Notes From Hampstead: The Writer's Notes: 1954–1971
fields.Author: Elias Canetti
fields.Role_in_Set: Source check: published English of the note Földényi retranslates from German.
fields.Selection_Logic: Földényi n. 1 cites Nachträge aus Hampstead p. 32.
fields.Quotes: “I have often considered it the most important book I know.” (1960, after the note on Pavese)
fields.Themes: Bushman folklore; Pavese; retranslation

fields.Title: The Intellectuals and the Masses: Pride and Prejudice Among the Literary Intelligentsia 1880-1939
fields.Author: John Carey
fields.Role_in_Set: Day 3 primary (argues with): ch. 1 'The Revolt of the Masses', the Canetti passage and n. 11.
fields.Selection_Logic: Day-2 lead; 14 'Canetti' all in one argued passage: a thesis against Crowds and Power, not a mention.
fields.Quotes:
“Elias Canetti, generally cited as the most profound modern commentator on the mass, stands at the end of the ‘scientific’ tradition stretching from Le Bon to Freud, and inherits its fantasies and confusions.” (ch. 1)
“It is presumably this dual awareness that accounts for the ambivalence that runs through Canetti’s Masse und Macht, and disturbs its intellectual coherence.” (ch. 1)
“In these respects Canetti’s crowd is virtually identical with Le Bon’s. Yet Canetti also envisages the crowd as the salvation of mankind.” (ch. 1)
“So in Canetti’s logic the crowd is both a subhuman monster and a community offering human fellowship and resistance to tyranny.” (ch. 1)
“Intellectuals believe in giving the public what intellectuals want; that, generally speaking, is what they mean by education.” (ch. 1)
fields.Themes: intellectuals and the masses; Le Bon; Freud; crowd as mob; newspapers; class contempt

fields.Title: Plasticity: The Promise of Explosion (catalogued as 'Plasticity at the Dusk of Writing')
fields.Author: Catherine Malabou (ed. Tyler M. Williams; ch. 8 tr. Dashiell Wasserman)
fields.Role_in_Set: Day 3 primary (argues with): ch. 8 'The Crowd: Figuring the Democracy to Come', pp. 115–129.
fields.Selection_Logic: 51 'Canetti' concentrated in ch. 8; argues against the mob reading (Negri) and so against Carey's kind of reading. Calibre metadata wrong: the file is the 2022 Edinburgh UP collection (ISBN 978 1 4744 6211 2).
fields.Quotes:
“Readers of Canetti have never, to my knowledge, insisted on this disparity; instead they see in the concept of the mass a sort of formless swarming that the English call a ‘mob’, a conglomerate without organisation.” (p. 117)
“It seems to me, on the contrary, that nothing is more organised than the mass that Canetti describes” (p. 117)
“I am aware, here, that I am making Canetti’s book talk and perhaps making it say more than it would on its own.” (p. 118)
“Democracy is the mass’s tact.” (p. 118)
“The goal is the most intense darkness where the most people are gathered.” (p. 115, as quoted; Stewart: ‘This goal is the blackest spot where most people are gathered.’)
fields.Themes: crowd; mass; democracy to come; tact; Derrida; Negri; metamorphosis; masks; secrecy; back-translation

fields.Title: George Steiner at the New Yorker
fields.Author: George Steiner (ed. Robert Boyers)
fields.Year: 2009 ('A Tale of Three Cities', New Yorker, 22 Nov 1982)
fields.Role_in_Set: Day 3 primary (argues with): 'A Tale of Three Cities', review of The Torch in My Ear (index pp. 260–69). Duplicate record 11442.
fields.Selection_Logic: 70 'Canetti'; the only one of the day's books to argue with Canetti's rank and conduct; its block quotations are checkable against 421.
fields.Quotes:
“He has rounded fiercely, and not altogether fairly, on those who—particularly in England, to which he came as a refugee—failed to keep his books in print”
“It would be 1960 before “Crowds and Power,” a torso of a work, fragmentary in its brilliance, appeared.”
“Nonetheless, it would be difficult to find anything in Canetti’s subsequent writings to match the powers of Opus I.”
“But there are no footnotes in this edition, and the translation is often ingeniously unhelpful.”
“With the current fading of psychoanalytic presumptions, it may well be these “refusers” of Freud who will prove lasting.”
“His exacting presence honors literature.”
fields.Themes: rank; Kafka; Broch; Kleist; Kraus; refusers of Freud; translation; Brand/Kant/Kien

fields.Title: Kafka's Other Trial: The Letters to Felice
fields.Author: Elias Canetti (tr. Christopher Middleton)
fields.Role_in_Set: Day 4 primary (Canetti as reader/rewriter of Kafka). Scan without text layer; OCR'd with tesseract for this run; printed page = PDF page − 4.
fields.Selection_Logic: Named in the week's plan for day 4: Canetti following Kafka through the Felice correspondence; its diary quotations can be checked against the library's Diaries (3169), the translation Canetti cites.
fields.Quotes:
“With the word Gerichtshof (“tribunal”), he had entered the sphere of the novel.” (p. 68)
“There is no external tribunal that he acknowledges; he is his own tribunal, but very much so, and that tribunal will always be in session.” (p. 70)
“As I was sitting down, I looked at her closely for the first time, by the time I was seated I already had an unshakable verdict.” (p. 5)
n. 50: “does not appear in the German Tagebiicher or in the English Diaries. The source is the manuscript of the diaries as cited by Klaus Wagenbach” (p. 121)
fields.Themes: tribunal; verdict; Felice; thinness; smallness; power; restoration of cut text

fields.Title: Franz Kafka: The Necessity of Form
fields.Author: Stanley Corngold
fields.Role_in_Set: Day 4 primary (translates Canetti afresh from Der andere Prozeß; quotes Neugroschel's Conscience of Words).
fields.Selection_Logic: Found by full-text search for “unerschütterliches Urteil” (2 hits); Mentions row 173 shows 13 Canetti mentions; all Kafka-book quotations are cited to the German Hanser 1969 edition, Middleton never cited.
fields.Quotes:
“what Elias Canetti calls Kafka’s “compulsive sacralization” of places and states of mind—which amounts to a “sacralization of man. Every place, every moment, every aspect, every step of the way is serious and important and unique.”” (Introduction, n. 8)
“an unshakeable judgment [unerschütterliches Urteil]” (ch. 2, citing DI 269)
“There is something deeply exciting about this stubborn attempt of someone who was helpless, to exclude himself from power in any form” (ch. 6, n. 22)
fields.Themes: retranslation; sacralization; judgment; power; Kafka scholarship

fields.Title: The Kraus Project
fields.Author: Karl Kraus, tr. and annotated by Jonathan Franzen (with Paul Reitter and Daniel Kehlmann)
fields.Role_in_Set: Day 4 primary (a translation/edition of Kraus whose annotator summarises Canetti on Kraus), set against Canetti's 'Karl Kraus: The School of Resistance' (413) and Torch 'Karl Kraus and Veza' (421).
fields.Selection_Logic: Day plan pointed to the Kraus chapters; The Last Days of Mankind (6351) was already used, so the library's other Kraus translation was searched: one Canetti mention, Reitter's n. 14 to 'Nestroy and Posterity'.
fields.Quotes:
“Elias Canetti, for example, argued that Kraus was too authoritarian a figure to encourage intellectual independence in other people, and that his style overwhelmed readers more than it stimulated their critical faculties.” (n. 14)
Canetti (413, pp. 35–36): “The heart of the matter was that he had appropriated all judging and did not permit anyone whose model he was to do any judging of his own.”
Canetti (421): “It was like a court of law. He brought the charges and he passed judgment. There was no defense attorney”
fields.Themes: Kraus; judgment; discipleship; dictatorship; paraphrase; self-indictment

fields.Title: Diaries, 1910-1923
fields.Author: Franz Kafka (tr. Joseph Kresh; Martin Greenberg with Hannah Arendt)
fields.Role_in_Set: Check text: the translation Canetti cites; used to verify every diary quotation in 3246 and Corngold's DI citation. Not a primary book.
fields.Selection_Logic: Canetti's notes cite Diaries I and II (Schocken 1948, 1949); 3169 is that translation.
fields.Quotes:
“As I was taking my seat I looked at her closely for the first time, by the time I was seated I already had an unshakeable opinion.” (20 Aug 1912)
“You sat as a judge over me in the Askanischer Hof - it was awful for you, for me, for everyone - but it only seemed so; in reality all the time I was sitting in your place and sit there to this day.” (1914)
fields.Themes: diary; Felice; tribunal; Brod's edition
